title: Model Question Paper 2
meta: Time: 3 hours · Maximum marks: 100 · Modelled on the April 2026 NIOS paper (new syllabus)
instructions: The question paper consists of 27 questions. All questions are compulsory; where there is an OR, answer one.
Questions 1–13 are objective (MCQ, True/False, match, fill in the blanks, one word) of 1 mark per part.
Questions 14–19 carry 2 marks (30–40 words). Question 21 has five parts of 2 marks. Questions 20 and 27 carry 3 marks, 22 and 24–26 carry 4 marks, and 23 carries 6 marks (150–200 words).
Questions from previous NIOS papers show the exam they appeared in.

sections.passage: Bal Gangadhar Tilak was born on July 23, 1856, in Ratnagiri, Maharashtra. His quest for knowledge led him to pursue higher education in mathematics and law. Tilak's entry into politics was marked by his deep sense of national pride and a call for Swaraj. He became a part of the Indian National Congress but later founded the extremist wing within the Congress, advocating a more assertive approach towards achieving independence. His newspapers, 'Kesari' and 'Maratha', became powerful platforms for spreading nationalist ideas. Tilak felt that the cultural and religious traditions of India were being suppressed. He decided to make the Ganesh Chaturthi celebration a public event, believing that by celebrating the festival openly and bringing people together, they could assert their cultural identity and build a sense of unity and pride. In 1895, Tilak organised a grand Shivaji festival in Pune to commemorate the Maratha warrior king. In a memorable public gathering, Tilak declared, "Swarajya is my birthright, and I shall have it!" This statement became a rallying cry for the independence movement. While imprisoned at Mandalay Central Jail in Burma, he wrote several works, including 'The Arctic Home in the Vedas' and 'Gita Rahasya'.

sections.passage:
Plastic was once hailed as a wonder material. It is light, cheap, strong and can be moulded into almost any shape. Today, however, the very qualities that made plastic popular have turned it into one of the world's biggest environmental problems. Because it is cheap, we use it carelessly and throw it away after a single use. Because it is durable, it does not rot; a plastic bottle may take hundreds of years to break down.

Much of this waste ends up in rivers and oceans. Sea turtles mistake floating bags for jellyfish, and seabirds feed bits of plastic to their chicks. Over time, plastic breaks into tiny pieces called microplastics, which have been found in fish, salt and even drinking water.

The solution does not lie in banning plastic altogether, for it is useful in medicine and many industries. It lies in using less of it, reusing what we can and recycling the rest. Carrying a cloth bag, refusing plastic straws and segregating waste at home may seem small steps, but when millions of people take them, the change is enormous.

questions.q: Modern public libraries offer only printed books.
Some libraries help senior citizens learn digital payments.
Mobile libraries take books to villages without a library.
'Little free libraries' charge a small fee for each book.
Librarians feel that the need for public libraries has decreased.

sections.passage: Libraries are no longer silent rooms full of dusty books. Many public libraries today offer free internet, e-books and audiobooks that members can borrow on their phones. Some run coding clubs for children, language classes for adults and help desks where senior citizens learn to use digital payments. Mobile libraries carry books in buses to villages that have no library of their own. In some cities, 'little free libraries' — small wooden boxes on street corners — invite people to take a book and leave a book. Librarians say that although reading habits have changed, the need for a friendly public space where anyone can learn, free of cost, has only grown.

sections.passage:
Leisure — W. H. Davies (lines)

What is this life if, full of care,
We have no time to stand and stare.
No time to stand beneath the boughs
And stare as long as sheep or cows.
No time to see, when woods we pass,
Where squirrels hide their nuts in grass.
No time to turn at Beauty's glance,
And watch her feet, how they can dance.

questions.q: 'Going to school was a turning point in Bholi's life.' Elaborate with examples from the story. (Bholi)
questions.answer: Before school Bholi was neglected, mocked and silent. Her teacher's kindness and the promise of reading gave her hope and confidence. Education helped her overcome her stammer, and in the end she spoke boldly, rejected a greedy groom and chose to teach and care for her parents.

or.q: Describe the change of heart in the bearded man. (Three Questions)
or.answer: He hated the king for executing his brother and seizing his property, and lay in wait to kill him. When the king tended his wound and saved his life, his hatred turned to gratitude. He begged forgiveness and vowed to serve the king; kindness turned an enemy into a friend.

sections.passage:
Meera ran a small tea stall at the bus stand of a hill town. Every morning she opened at five, when the first bus left for the plains. Students, drivers and labourers gathered around her stove, for her ginger tea was the best in town and she always had a kind word for everyone.

One monsoon night, a landslide blocked the only road. Nearly forty passengers were stranded at the bus stand, among them an old couple and a mother with a feverish baby. The nearest hotel was full. Meera did not think twice. She kept her stall open all night, boiled tea and khichdi on her single stove and refused to take money from anyone. She wrapped the baby in her own shawl and sent her son running through the rain to call the town's only doctor.

By morning the road was cleared. The passengers tried to pay her, but she laughed, "Tea tastes better when it is shared." A journalist among them wrote about her in a newspaper. A few weeks later the district administration honoured her and gave her a grant to build a small shelter at the bus stand. Meera named it 'Sabka Ghar' — everyone's home.

questions.q: Write an article (150–200 words) on 'The Importance of Physical Fitness for Young People'.
questions.answer:
The Importance of Physical Fitness for Young People
In an age of screens and fast food, physical fitness has become more important than ever for young people. Regular exercise keeps the heart and lungs healthy, builds strong muscles and bones, and prevents obesity and lifestyle diseases that are now appearing even in teenagers.
Fitness is not only about the body. Exercise releases chemicals in the brain that reduce stress and improve mood, concentration and sleep — a great help during examinations. Team sports teach discipline, cooperation, leadership and the grace to accept both victory and defeat.
Yet many students spend hours sitting with books or phones. Even thirty to sixty minutes a day of brisk walking, cycling, yoga, swimming or games can make a big difference. Schools should give games periods their due, and parents should encourage outdoor play instead of screen time.
A fit body supports an alert mind. If young people make fitness a daily habit now, they will enjoy healthier, happier and more productive lives.

or.q: Write a speech (150–200 words) for the morning assembly on 'Save Water'.
or.answer:
Good morning, respected Principal, teachers and dear friends.
Today I wish to speak on a resource we take for granted — water. Though three-fourths of the earth is water, only a tiny part is fresh and fit to drink. Many cities in India already face severe shortages, and groundwater is falling every year.
Much of this crisis is caused by waste. A dripping tap can waste thousands of litres a year; running taps while brushing, washing cars with hoses and leaking pipes all add to the loss.
We can make a difference. Turn off taps when not in use and repair leaks at once. Use a bucket instead of a hose, and reuse water from washing vegetables to water plants. Harvest rainwater on rooftops and in schools.
Let us remember: we cannot make water, we can only save it. Every drop saved today is a drop for tomorrow. Thank you.

or.q: Write a summary of the passage above (on sleep and health) in about 60 words.
or.answer: Sleep is vital for teenagers, who need eight to ten hours a night but usually get less. It helps the brain store learning and the body repair and grow. Too little sleep harms concentration, memory and mood, and is linked with obesity, diabetes and depression. Screens, homework, caffeine and irregular routines are the chief causes; a fixed bedtime, no screens and a quiet room help.

sections.passage: Sleep is as important to health as food and exercise. Teenagers need eight to ten hours of sleep each night, yet most get far less. During sleep the brain sorts and stores what was learnt during the day, so sleep is vital for memory and learning. The body repairs muscles, releases growth hormones and strengthens the immune system. Lack of sleep causes poor concentration, irritability, weak memory and more accidents; over time it is linked with obesity, diabetes and depression. The main causes of poor sleep among young people are late-night use of phones and screens, heavy homework, caffeine and irregular routines. Experts advise a fixed bedtime, no screens for an hour before sleep, a dark and quiet room, and avoiding tea, coffee and heavy meals late in the evening.

questions.q: A Yoga Shivir was organised by your colony on 21st June, International Day of Yoga. Write a news clipping for the Residents' Welfare Association in about 120 words. (Report Writing)
questions.answer:
YOGA SHIVIR DRAWS HUNDREDS
By Rohan Mehra, Shanti Vihar

On International Day of Yoga, 21 June, the Shanti Vihar RWA organised a Yoga Shivir in the community park from 6 to 8 a.m. Over 250 residents of all ages took part.
Yoga teacher Ms Anjali Sen led sessions on surya namaskar, pranayama and meditation, and explained how daily practice reduces stress and lifestyle diseases. Senior citizens were given simple chair exercises.
"I feel fresh and energetic," said 72-year-old Mr Gupta. Children enjoyed a special session of animal poses.
The RWA has decided to hold free yoga classes every Sunday morning.
